title: Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems

concept.text: The innovation would be an explicit deterministic algorithm that solves an NP-complete problem, such as Boolean satisfiability or 3-SAT, correctly on every input in proved polynomial time, with costs small enough for practical use. Satisfiability asks whether values can be assigned to Boolean variables so that a given logical formula is true. An algorithm meeting this goal would provide a general way to find satisfying assignments or determine that none exist, including on difficult instances rather than only selected families.

P is the class of decision problems solvable in deterministic polynomial time: the running time is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the encoded input length. NP consists of decision problems whose YES answers have polynomially bounded witnesses that can be checked in polynomial time. NP-complete problems are sufficiently expressive that every problem in NP can be translated into them with polynomial overhead. Consequently, a polynomial-time algorithm for one NP-complete problem would establish P = NP and yield polynomial-time methods for the associated witness-search problems.

Practicality is an additional requirement beyond the mathematical statement P = NP. A polynomial algorithm can have an enormous degree, large constants, or expensive translations from applications. This concept therefore requires both a rigorous worst-case guarantee and a usable implementation. It concerns the efficiency of solving already decidable problems; it would not make arbitrary mathematical questions decidable.

significance.text: The direct consequence would be a broad expansion of efficient computation wherever candidate solutions have short, efficiently checkable descriptions. Suitable formulations of scheduling, routing, layout and other combinatorial tasks would acquire general polynomial-time solution methods. For optimization problems, the consequence applies where feasibility questions, objective bounds and solution recovery admit suitable polynomial-size encodings. The revolutionary feature would be the transfer of one algorithmic advance across many problem domains through reductions.

Bounded formal proof search would also benefit. When a formal proof can be checked efficiently, searching for a proof within a specified polynomially bounded length fits the witness-search framework. This could substantially expand automated reasoning within those bounds. It would not guarantee short proofs of every true statement, eliminate undecidability, or remove the need to choose useful mathematical questions and representations.

Cryptographic consequences would extend beyond NP-complete problems themselves. Although integer factoring and discrete logarithms are not known to be NP-complete, their efficiently verifiable search formulations can be reduced to satisfiability. A polynomial-time SAT algorithm would therefore yield polynomial-time algorithms for them as well. Cook explicitly describes recovering integer factors through an NP decision problem. Whether the resulting attacks would be practical would depend on reduction overhead and implementation costs. This creates a direct overlap with MAT-06.

The analogy between polynomial time and routine computation has important limits. Input encoding, reduction costs, witness lengths, memory requirements, polynomial degree and constants all affect practical performance. A fast method for a compact SAT instance need not translate into an equally fast method for an application whose encoding becomes much larger. Dias and Lima's analysis of a claimed subexponential satisfiability result illustrates the separate issue of asymptotic improvement versus feasible-size benefit; it does not establish the correctness of the underlying claim.

A proof that P ≠ NP would be a different fundamental achievement. It would establish that NP-complete problems lack deterministic polynomial-time algorithms in the worst case, but would not imply that every instance or every present computation is difficult. It would also not, by itself, establish the average-case hardness needed for cryptographic security or prove that one-way functions exist.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a constructive, deterministic method that handles all instances of an NP-complete problem within a proved polynomial bound. Decades of algorithmic work and efforts to prove complexity lower bounds have not supplied an accepted resolution. Success on selected instances, particular distributions or restricted structural families does not establish the necessary worst-case guarantee. Conversely, the absence of an accepted polynomial algorithm is not a proof that such an algorithm cannot exist.

The mathematical barrier is to supply an algorithm and an analysis that bound every part of its computation, including difficult cases, by a fixed polynomial in a clearly defined input length. An improvement that remains superpolynomial would not establish P = NP, even if it substantially improved existing asymptotic bounds. Cook's discussion also distinguishes an existence argument for P = NP from an algorithm that could feasibly solve standard NP-complete problems.

Engineering synthesis: turning such a theorem into this practical innovation would require controlling constants, memory use, representation size and the cost of translating real problems into the algorithm's input format. The implementation would need to preserve the assumptions used in the proof, including its treatment of arithmetic and intermediate data. A theoretically polynomial core would be insufficient if preprocessing, output recovery or application encodings made the complete workflow unusable.

The barriers analyzed by Dias and Lima should not be generalized into an impossibility result for this innovation. Their lower bounds concern a specified clause-product scheme under a particular cost model. Their scope excludes the original preprint's parity and tensor-contraction routes. Those restrictions matter: a limitation of one computational construction is not a lower bound against every possible SAT algorithm.

current_state.text: Cook proved satisfiability and 3-SAT NP-complete in 1971. Levin independently developed related universal-search results; Cook's historical account cites Levin's publication as appearing in 1973. These foundations establish why solving one NP-complete problem in polynomial time would transfer to all of NP. They do not establish a practical polynomial-time algorithm.

The supplied review reports that the saved Clay Mathematics Institute overview, retrieved on 11 November 2026, presents P versus NP as unsolved. This supports the absence of an accepted general polynomial-time solution at that snapshot. The overview supplies a status statement rather than a new technical proof. Because the supplied freshness-search record is empty, it does not independently establish the problem's status specifically on 1 November 2026.

The research describes modern solvers as successful on many practical instances, but the supplied evidence does not document a contemporary benchmark range, comparative performance or a worst-case complexity analysis for those solvers. That practical-success statement therefore remains qualitative here. Selected-instance success would not settle P versus NP, and the problem's unresolved status does not itself prove a superpolynomial lower bound for every practical solver.

In a note submitted on 31 October 2026, Fabio Dias and Yvens Lima analyze an OpenAI preprint that they report was posted on 17 October and revised on 25 October. They describe a claimed deterministic subexponential counting bound that would refute the Exponential Time Hypothesis if correct. Their note takes the original proofs at face value and expressly does not assess their correctness. The original OpenAI preprint is absent from the supplied materials, so its claims and dates are represented through this analysis rather than through direct examination.

Dias and Lima conclude that the extracted guarantees certify no speed-up over brute force for bounded-density formulas at any size that could feasibly be written down. This is a conclusion about what the analyzed bounds guarantee, not a measurement showing that every actual run is slower than brute force. Their method-specific lower bounds also leave the parity and tensor-contraction routes outside their scope. A subexponential bound alone does not establish a polynomial-time algorithm or settle P versus NP.

Evidence limitation: the research also mentions a secondary explainer dated 15 October 2026 and updated 28 October, but that article is absent from the supplied sources. Its dates, contents and characterization of the claims cannot be independently established from this record, so it supplies no additional status evidence here. This missing access does not show that the article or the underlying algorithmic claim is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mathematical demonstration: publish an explicit deterministic algorithm for 3-SAT or another NP-complete problem, accompanied by a proof of correctness on every valid input and an explicit polynomial worst-case time bound. The statement should specify the computational model, input-size measure, encoding, arithmetic costs and assumptions. Refereeing and independent scrutiny would help establish confidence in the proof; these are proposed criteria for this record, not an asserted consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed mathematical demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed implementation demonstration: release public code whose operations can be connected to the proved algorithm and resource bound. Provide reproducible build instructions, hardware and software configurations, input generators or shareable benchmark instances, and complete runtime and memory measurements. Demonstrate useful performance on previously intractable industrial instances at sizes where credible contemporary solvers fail under comparable resource limits.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed implementation demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth and reproducibility demonstration: have independent groups reproduce the proof analysis and implementation results across varied instance families, including difficult satisfiable and unsatisfiable cases. Report failures, crossover sizes and the costs of application reductions and witness recovery. Finite benchmarks would establish demonstrated breadth and practical boundaries; correctness and the universal worst-case bound would still depend on the mathematical proof.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed breadth and reproducibility demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope boundary: a nonconstructive existence proof without a feasible algorithm, a superpolynomial improvement whose benefits appear only at astronomical sizes, or a proof that P ≠ NP would not complete this particular innovation. Nor would strong benchmark performance without the required all-input polynomial guarantee. The distinction between resolving P versus NP and obtaining a feasible algorithm is grounded in Cook's account; the combined proof-and-performance requirements here are proposals.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed scope boundary

related_concepts.text: MAT-06, Classical polynomial-time integer factorization and discrete logarithms, has direct computational overlap. A polynomial-time SAT algorithm would yield polynomial-time methods for these verifiable search problems through reductions, despite their not being known NP-complete. MAT-06 remains distinct because a specialized factoring or discrete-logarithm algorithm would not by itself establish P = NP, and it might have different practical costs.

Roster-based synthesis: MAT-05, Research-scale machine-checked mathematical discovery, overlaps through bounded formal proof search. MAT-01 could provide a powerful search component when proofs have manageable lengths and efficient verification. MAT-05 additionally concerns research-scale discovery and checking workflows; a polynomial-time search theorem alone would not ensure useful conjectures, short proofs or productive mathematical judgment.

Roster-based synthesis: MAT-09, Classical polynomial-time algorithms for cryptographic lattice problems, overlaps where a particular lattice task has a polynomially bounded, efficiently verifiable witness formulation. MAT-01 could address such formulations through reductions, while MAT-09 concerns the specific lattice problems and guarantees needed for that separate innovation. Their relationship must be assessed for each problem variant and parameter regime rather than inferred from the word 'cryptographic.'

Roster-based synthesis: MAT-04, Proved polynomial-cost solution of high-dimensional nonlinear PDEs, and MAT-08, Polynomial-time chemical accuracy for molecular electronic structure, share an interest in controlling computational cost. Their guarantees additionally depend on numerical representation, precision, approximation error and the relevant physical problem class. MAT-01 would transfer only where an appropriate finite formulation and efficiently verifiable witness exist with manageable encoding costs; it would not automatically supply either roster entry's full numerical guarantee.

Roster-based synthesis: MAT-02, An effective global Langlands correspondence over number fields, could intersect with MAT-01 through suitably bounded proof searches or finite computational subproblems. Its central objective is an effective mathematical correspondence. Efficient solution of NP problems would not by itself establish that correspondence or provide its required constructions.

Roster-based synthesis: MAT-03, A first-principles theory of turbulent transport, and MAT-07, A prescriptive mathematical theory of deep learning, could benefit from faster combinatorial searches within particular formulations. Their principal goals concern explanatory and predictive theories. Efficient search alone would not supply a validated transport theory, a theory of learning, or the assumptions connecting either theory to observed behavior.

change_log.reason: NP-completeness is unnecessary for reduction to SAT. The review identifies efficiently verifiable search formulations and Cook's explicit factoring construction.

change_log.change: Defined P and NP as decision-problem classes and specified polynomially bounded witnesses.
change_log.reason: This preserves the distinction between deciding a problem and recovering a witness while explaining the conditional transfer to associated search problems.

unresolved_issues: The original OpenAI preprint is absent. Its correctness, exact statements and reported posting and revision dates cannot be independently assessed from the supplied record.
The supplied review establishes an analysis of certified bounds, not actual performance measurements for every implementation or input.
No supplied contemporary benchmarks substantiate the breadth or limits of modern practical solver performance.
The secondary explainer mentioned in the research is absent, leaving its dates and contents unverified.
The Clay snapshot was retrieved on 11 November 2026; the empty freshness-search record leaves exact status on 1 November unverified.
Acceptable polynomial degrees, constants, memory budgets, benchmark families and practical crossover sizes remain to be specified for the proposed completion demonstration.
Relationships with roster entries other than the directly supported factoring and witness-search consequences remain conceptual and depend on each entry's precise formulations and guarantees.
